nottherightfounder.title: Not the Right Founderâ€”Yet
nottherightfounder.heading: Not the Right Founderâ€”Yet
content:
I am a founder and people say that I am a young founder and I sometimes tend to agree with them (I am 21 while writing this).
I graduated from college this month and this is my 2nd startup (first Svar and now Aiva). I've pitched to dozens of investors, tried raising money for both, and whatever small wins I've had, I still wouldn't call it "raising a round."

I got $30K for Svar, but from competitions and grants, not investors. Sometimes, it's "you are too early", sometimes "small TAM", and several other stuff that investors say. And I realise these are things investors say to get around and dodge. It's never too early, it's never a small TAM, it's never the market or stage or product really. People raise pre-product, they raise in niche businesses. It's always, the Founder. It's always "You are not right for us, yet".

And I have been used to listening, "Sorry, We have decided to pass", and now it goes into my ears like - "You are not the right founder, yet". The Yet.
That yet used to sting. Now I'm starting to appreciate it. Because they're rightâ€”I haven't earned it yet. I'm not the founder who makes it a no-brainer. Not the one who walks into the room and flips the question from "Why should we invest?" to "How can we not?"
Not yet.
Right now, not even I can say that for myself :). And I am ready to take accountability for that, I won't be blind.

Everytime, I realise, I am not yet the guy who can sell a concept. And this is what I am really loving about building a startup. Love the mirror it always keeps in front of you if you decide to untie the blindfold from your eyes.

And I love the opportunity it presents. The rejections I face always end with a "Yet". I am not a great founder, yet. I am not the best seller, yet. I am not the right guy to invest in, yet. I am becoming that founder, past the yet. There will always be more to learn, I am getting past "more yets" everyday. Love it.
I also worry, what would have happened if I hadn't started up out of courage or naivety, whichever is the case with me ðŸ˜€. I wouldn't have known how many yets there are in my life.
Love it.
Thanks for reading.

dontsweat.title: Don't Sweat the Small Stuff - Ujjwal Mathur
dontsweat.heading: Don't Sweat the Small Stuff
content: This essay is directly a praise of "Don't Sweat the Small Stuff... and It's all small stuff" by Dr Richard Carlson. I read it recently and it's been one of the simplest and best reads I've had.

Reading about the "small stuff" made me question myself and observe my own behaviour towards it. How do I handle the "small stuff" ? Just every other person. Making a big deal about the small stuff. I noticed that I live life like a big emergency, and consider every event or task like a must complete or must win task.

Now, a perspective is that winning these small events eventually fetches big results, and that's very true. In no way, I am denying that. However, what I am pointing out is how we make a big deal about the results of the events, after they are done or the time has passed by. Even during the event, we extract the joy out of it, worrying, and meanwhile deprive ourselves from participating in other things.

A cliche example, preparing for an exam. This happens way too often with me. If I have an exam the day after tomorrow, and my friend calls me for an hour of gym or FIFA session, I always deny, only to later waste 2 hours on "miscellaneous" activity that I don't have any account for. It's just that I won't have the "guilt" that I went for FIFA and that I wasted my time. Haha, funny nature of mine. Please smile if you can relate to this funny nature. Well, personally, this is not just about exams, but a lot many parts of my day, and only on self-introspection I observed this in myself.

This abstract concept of sweating about small stuff or wins can be easily expanded to a range of behavioural traits. Think of a time when someone was telling a story or sharing an achievement, how we often immediately tried to share something about ourselves. Just pause and think.
Smile again if you can relate. I can totally relate. This is just human nature, everyone wants attention and wants to feel important or special. We can try to be easy sometimes, and let it go.
Let Others Have the Glory.

Richard Carlson has talked about a lot of relatable small stuff that we sweat about in his "Don't Sweat the Small Stuff... and it's all small stuff". A good and small read that triggers self-introspection.
You may read my How to not sweat the small stuff to continue on this.
Thank You for reading.

softskills.title: Hard Skills or Soft Skills - Ujjwal Mathur
softskills.heading: Hard Skills or Soft Skills
content: I was reading Sam Altman's blog, "How to be successful", and never once did he mention a hard skill (or the importance of any hard skill to master) to focus on. There were points like compounding, self-belief, drive, etc. and the one that best matches the criterion of hard skill was, "be good as sales".
Anyone would follow Sam's advice to be successful, so let's treat his advice as if it's set in stone.

So, roughly, the skills to focus are soft skills, yet nowhere around me at least I see people working on or even discussing these. Nobody mentions that we should be really internally driven, or should focus on independent thinking. Mostly we are talking about what skill to get good at, like programming or design.

But let's leave this topic aside of why we don't discuss or not focus on that. Let's say I've figured out that I need to really focus on being driven, being self-confident and learning independent thinking. And this is really good advice, and great to hear in principle, but how do I really do it in practice?
I actually got to thinking about this and then decided to write about it.
How do we learn independent thinking, really ? What's step 1 or step x, anything ?

Maybe building things is one way. I have a very rough idea and that's because I've thought about it up until this point and I believe thinking more will get me more ideas. The best thing about reading such stuff from great people is that it reminds me of this "actually" important stuff.

On the contrary, I remember what Ben Horowitz says in "The hard thing about hard things", that there is no playbook for doing hard things, and maybe learning independent thinking is a "hard thing". Maybe, I am just digging dry ground trying to find this way of learning these things. But still, a starting point would be good at least.
I'll think more. I really wanted if I could discuss such things with friends here in college. Anyways, I hope work life is better at this.
Until then, thanks Sam. Will thank you in person soon. Haha, self-belief I guess :).
Thank You for Reading.
Oh, read Sam's blog here - https://blog.samaltman.com/how-to-be-successful

whyblogs.title: Why Blogs? - Ujjwal Mathur
whyblogs.heading: Why Blogs?
content: This is a thought that comes very often to people, at least it came to me a lot. Why should I read? Why does someone write? Well, it's trivial why you should read and write if you are in school or college, but other than that why should a 25-year-old read or even an undergrad read something that's not gonna earn them grades or pleasure 🙂. I already had an argument against reading, that it's boring, and that was a big argument to me at the time.

Before I give an arguably good answer or an answer at least, well, even I discovered the answer to this less than a year and a half ago when I started to read forcefully, yes forcefully. This happened because I was overly fascinated by the thought of being an avid reader. I was coming across this way too often on my social media feed - Instagram, X (then Twitter), LinkedIn, and even Reddit, which I used rarely, but enough to come across this idea. Although I was never a reader, preferred to watch videos instead of reading articles, watch movies instead of novels, I liked the idea of being a reader.

I thought and still believe that many people find it a cool personality trait. And as Jay Shetty writes You are not what you think you are, you are what you think people think you are. And since people find it cool (as per my belief), I wanted to build this habit. Another reason was that I had heard and read (surprisingly) that reading leads to knowledge, and I wanted to be knowledgeable. This desire to be knowledgeable also wasn't my own, instead because again I liked this trait in some of my friends who could debate (even after a certain point) about history, ideologies, and current affairs. So, both these reasons led to me starting "Dogalapan".

Yes, Dogalapan was my first book. I don't remember why I chose it, but in hindsight, it looks like an interesting choice to me. Well, I already liked Ashneer Grover back then from his "performance" in Shark Tank Season 1 and 2, so it was easy to start the book. The first few chapters were all about setting the plot for his "triumph", and they helped me realize that I like stories. The way the Baniya household tales were narrated had me and made the first quarter smooth to read, and I would get par the daily goal of 15 pages a day (as per my feed) quite easily.

However, I got bored soon and now started to read in broken stints. 5 pages a day or 10 pages a day went on for some days. And then that was it. I could no longer bear the boringness. Although my feed had told me that consistency is the key and that a habit does not develop overnight, it was overpowered by the boring nature of reading and overshadowed by the interesting hostel activities, and so I quit reading. By the time I quit, I had already reached the so-called most interesting part of the book, the climax, or the anti-climax in this case, I guess the climax of Dogalapan showed Dogalapan. Anyway, it couldn't stop me from abolishing the PDF file that remained open on Microsoft Edge (I didn't want the guilt of quitting).

The hostel activities (and the academics 🙂) got me busy, and the impulsive desire to be cool went dormant or ignored for some days. A month later, another impulsive desire to change my life or make a comeback (as the Instagram reels portray it) hit me. And guess what, I opened Microsoft Edge, which I had been ignoring for the last few weeks. "Small things make large", and so I started reading where I left off - "Sir, 116 par khula hai share (The share has listed at 116)", I read. I don't remember how much I read in a go, but it was a good stint I can recall. I felt good, because I read, and believed that I was doing something productive, although I could nowhere see how it was, but it felt good.

The desire was strong enough to complete the book, the last 3 chapters of the book, and this time I very proudly closed the tab, and finally I had finished my first book. Can I call myself a reader, "Not yet", I said, "but, I can after a few books", I replied to myself and went out of my room with a smile on my face, with the very important hostel activities of that day. I wish I had noted down the date.

Well, excited about my accomplishment, I started looking for my next book to conquer. I consulted Guruji - my wingmate (hostel gives you these names), who possessed this extremely cool trait. He was of no help, however, and I, on my own, landed up on Stay Hungry, Stay Foolish - The Inspiring Stories of 25 IIM Ahmedabad graduates who chose to tread a path of their own making, by Rashmi Bansal. Why this one? Because I had just realized that I liked stories and this one had a lot of them. My summer vacation had started, and I read this one in a jiffy, a couple of weeks I guess. And voila, I had the dopamine kick in. While I was reading this book, I realized that not just any stories, I liked life stories, especially inspiring ones. So halfway through the book, I downloaded my next one - Dream with Your Eyes Open - the autobiography of Ronnie Screwvala. I didn't much about the guy, had just heard his name because he was the co-owner of U Mumba, the kabaddi team. It was a life story, and hopefully an inspiring one, so I went on with it.

This one took some time, but now I was developing a habit slowly, so it felt good. I wasn't reading daily, but I was reading and progressing, and yeah it started to feel cool and had now become less boring. I went on and started to develop the habit of reading almost daily with the next books I read. Not that I had become fond of reading or was excited to do it every day, but I did it forcefully sometimes, because consistency is the key and it is indeed I realized gradually.

Haven't completed every book I started. It's been more than a year, and I have developed a habit of reading. I might not be an avid reader, but I am a reader now, I like to read. Reading has become more interesting and convenient for me now, more than watching YouTube videos, I like to read entire Wikipedia pages and news articles. I haven't read any novels yet, but I am not skeptical about it or argue against it. Yeah, once I watch a movie or a video on some real-life figure, I want to read all the articles on them available on Google.

By the way, did we forget the question?  Why read? Well, Reading is productive in my opinion. It increases your knowledge base, enriches your vocabulary, improves focus, etc. but above all, for me, it gives you perspectives, it unlocks your ability to think. And when you think, you develop the ability to articulate your thoughts. You might have heard Ben Shapiro or Donald Trump or Andrew Tate, how well they speak, not just that, the content they deliver, Sublime! Starting to read might be your way to reach that stage. It has worked for me at least, not up to that level yet of course, but I can now articulate my thoughts and speak in discussions (debates :)), and judging from people's reactions, it's not crap.

For me, reading is the reason why I have developed a desire to write. I read books, and think about the stuff written, and sometimes I cannot appreciate enough the writing styles of authors. I am often particularly impressed by how well they are able to portray in words what they think and believe. It becomes so impressive sometimes, often characterized by the feeling - "Wait, that's exactly what I feel sometimes" or "That's so what happens with me", "How did you put that in words", the aha moments, those lines just remain with you for a long time. The articulation just seems oddly satisfying sometimes, appears to me of the level that they have expressed something from their explicit memory. Notice that sometimes an idea is very hard to put in words, but easy to express with a drawing, it gets to that level but with words.

Some of my the books I read, the Psychology of Money, Ikigai, Zero to One, Never split the difference, were really good read, one either put thoughts into words so gracefully or one forced me to really think about it and in some cases change my perspective on that.

And that has sparked the desire in me to write. So much that one of the items in my lifetime bucket list is Writing a book, a good book, in the sense that I can build on my thoughts and draw them on paper, and not just me but the readers can see it, feel it.
And that's why, blogs!
Thank You for reading.

odds.title: What are my odds of making it? - Ujjwal Mathur
odds.heading: What are my odds of making it?
content: There are so few people in the world that are going to be successful, so few, you can literally count them, and it wouldn't even take a day. There are just 2,640 billionaires in the whole world. Such a small number. There were more people probably in your school or college. Not saying that becoming a billionaire is the only measure of success. But think of success, in whatever terms or form you see fit, in an analogous way. Fame? How many people are or have ever been famous. I think whether someone has a Wikipedia page or not is a fair measure to decide if someone's is famous (enough). There are a little over 1 million people (dead and alive) "registered as famous" on Wikipedia. And how many humans have ever lived? 117 billion.

What are the odds? 0.000008547. That's 0.0008547 percent of all the people. You probably didn't count the zeroes. That's how it is. But wait a sec. How many people do you think or I think know Gavrilo Princip? How many people do you think know Monti Panesar? Not a history test. But Gavrilo Princip was one of the key people in World War I. Monti Panesar played over 50 test matches for the English National Cricket Team. You know what are the odds of being selected for that. I happen to just know these names because I am interested in History and Cricket, but the thing is we hardly know 2000 or so people on that famous list on Wikipedia. Well, I guess this measure fails. Say someone knows 10,000 names on that list, that makes the ratio, haha, 0.00000008547. I guess fame is even worse than the "billionaires" measure.

Yes, Success is subjective. But thinking of success as being healthy, wealthy, and wise, is beyond the scope of this blog. But Everyone will accept that the two measures, money and fame, are indeed measures of success, not exhaustive obviously.
Why did I start writing about this? I was actually thinking what are the odds I make it. A cliche thought, a lot of people have this obviously, but they react to this in some way or the other.
The Three gunas or modes of life, as per Bhagavad Gita are Tamas, Rajas, and Sattva. How you respond to situations.

Tamas is Ignorance, ah you just ignore the thought and continue scrolling, a very probable trigger to this thought is social media, the causation need not be immediate but I believe there is a causation relation (mentioning this from personal experience and no credible backing, but just believe that this happens with a lot of people). So, you keep scrolling.

Rajas is Impulsive. You impulsively react (and not respond) to the stimulus (the urge here). You probably procrastinate, make some plans, get fired up, take a few actions, probably hit some pushups, set a few alarms, sometimes actually follow a routine of some sort for a week, and that's it. You keep scrolling.
Sattva is Goodness. You actually take action. You do the scrolling, but you do not "just keep scrolling".
Not a blog to fire you up. You may think about the question yourself and respond your way.

I just wanted to bring the attention to "What are the odds". I don't know what it takes to be "successful". It surely takes something. No doubt, it gives room for failures, it gives time, but hell yeah it takes a lot of efforts. Something that is so improbable to achieve must take something. Not a direct and fair comparison, but think of how difficult are Gaokao and JEE to pass, that have around 0.25% and 1% acceptance rate respectively. And then see where on the number line does 0.0008547(%) lie. It's insane, and beyond a certain order we do not realise the giganticness of something, like here the number. We know it's difficult, but we do not and we cannot feel how tough it is. Probably because we have a small imagination range of our emotions.

We gotta accept, it's hard. And everyone knows that. But where I think the question gets hidden from the sight of the people, is that we do not look at things zoomed out. We live (or exist, if not live) in the moment, look at things at the moment, and plan in the moment. Instead, the only thing we have to do in the moment, is act in the moment, and act in real not our thoughts. Zooming out is specifically important in my opinion. Words like hindsight and retrospective are two of my favorite words, because I like the positivity of looking at things zoomed out. They get you in a deep state of thoughts, sometimes in serenity, with reduced noise. We generally think this way, with muted noise, due to some stimulus. Like being on the mountains, or watching some inspiring interview, or some pivot points in life, like the demise of someone close.

People, especially in their 20s (including myself), often doubt themselves and worry about things, in retrospect and in the moment. But zooming out more often clears one's thought. I am saying this from both personal experience and articles I read, from some great authors.
The takeaway for me from this blog is the importance of the question, "What are the odds" and the emphasis it puts on the established "fact", it must take something, we gotta do that.
Some byproducts I feel can be - Sattva, Zooming out, and acting in the moment and for real.
Thank you for reading.

greatest.title: Who are the greatest sportsperson? - Ujjwal Mathur
greatest.heading: Who are the greatest sportsperson of all time ?
content: I am very confused right now, I just saw a clip on LinkedIn, an interview of Novak Djokovic. I always chose Rafa over Novak, so personally, I didn't like him. And especially when he surpassed Rafa for the "most grand slams for an individual" record. I kinda disliked him, and then I sympathized with myself, because this had happened with me before. Technically, not with me, but people I admired and some whom even I idealised. Cristiano was surpassed by Messi for the most Ballon D'ors. Lebron, very arguably, surpassed Jordan, a lot of people do not agree with this and even I don't, Michael is still THE basketball icon for me. But the fact that he was The basketball icon for everyone. Floyd surpassed Ali and Tyson, and similarly many others. I had seen this, my hero becoming number 2, and that led to a lot of people disrespecting them, specially on social media. I didn't like this, and I sympathised with myself for being the victim here.

Initially, I disliked and sometimes even hated these greats, especially Messi, because his claim was the strongest among all the other surpassers, especially with the World Cup. But I came to realize and acknowledge the greatness, not just of my heroes and those who surpassed them, but also of others who are deemed greats, those who have done what others could not have done (subjectively). "You have got to acknowledge them", I said to myself once in thought. You cannot forget Maradona. You cannot forget Agassi. You cannot not acknowledge Kobe. You simply cannot. These people are the greatest people in the areas they set their foot in, accept it or not.
There cannot be many "greatest", oh I am not making a grammatical error, I will address that.

But the thing I stuck with me, was the moment I realised that I have to accept them. How do you prove Messi is greater than Ronaldo? It's very very subjective, the golden balls do not define who's better, people vote for it, it depends on people, and the moment something depends on people, it becomes who's more likable, and not better. I am not defending Cristiano here, he might or might not be the greatest. Messi might be a greater footballer, and even Maradona might be the greatest. Who decides that? The super ballon d'or was given to Stefano and he played in the same era as Pele and Maradona, and he was nowhere in the Player of the century debate. Maradona won the player of the 20th century award when over 50 percent of people voted for him. Then a football committee voted Pele as the best, with over 70 percent votes. But wait Pele won 3 world cups, the most by anyone ever, ever. Then why isn't he the best till date? Probably because nobody who is alive today has seen him play, well that's the internet nature of people's perception.

The crux is, at least what I believe in, we/one cannot decide who's the greatest in such fields, given there is so much subjectivity, the voters, the parameters, the weights of parameters. Ah, we/one cannot. I don't know why this superlative was defined, or it was termed by the self proclaimed wannabes, I don't know. But the way I think about it, is we can define a pool of greatests, and that pool, a very small one can be called The Greatest (as a metaphor). Don't take it wrong, this isn't like the hall of fame with a hundred people in it. It's too large to be even called a group, so, pool.

Cristiano, Leo, Pele, Messi get in. Sorry Zizou, sorry Eusebio and Baggio. Jordan, Lebron, Kobe get in there. Probably even Bill Russel. I am not randomly naming athletes, instead I thought of who can be in this pool. People who are strongly in the goat race might be the ones. A subjective parameter again. But you see, I am not trying to be specific to names or individuals. Just like when I wanted Cristiano to win the debate, I blindly wanted that. But now, I might even accept a pool with no Cristiano in it, some day. Because I simply cannot admire an individual more than the idea of The Greatest pool. The pool stands out among the plethora of humans competing. And the core idea or trait, common among all the pools, think beyond sports, is greatness.

Abruptly, but getting back to the clip I saw. It was Novak speaking about his or greats' mentality. He said there is no room for doubts, no second thoughts, you have to believe in yourself, like insanely, and that he said is the difference, he thinks, between people who are and who are not at the highest level. Brutal, but probably the truth. That put me into an internal discussion, there must be so many people who have had this mentality and who are not among the greats', let alone the pool. I think these people in the pool might not be the best people to listen to when talking about the non-negotiables about reaching that level, just as IITians are not the best people to listen to for clearing IIT, a more relatable example. Not saying they are wrong, but just trying to establish explicitly that they do not have the mantras. Because whenever you listen to the interviews of these people, Kobe, Novak, Floyd, it gets you fired up, gets me too, and it feels like you have figured out the key, but I don't believe that. I think it's just the adrenaline that gets us overwhelmed, and out of reality…..   To be continued
Thank you for reading.

settling.title: Why do we settle for less? - Ujjwal Mathur
settling.heading: Why do we settle for less?
content: First things first. One wants love and appreciation from people, right?
People want to win, right? Everyone wants to win. And what does success demand? Efforts. On and off the field.

But we can often see people settling for sympathy. What does sympathy demand? Efforts. On the field. Although I have had just a handful of experiences around here. I mean I am 21, far away from the extremely experienced people you would read sharing their perspectives. But this scenario is so common that even a guy who hasn't even casted his first vote can say this. I do see people settling. Settling for less. If not success, then sympathy. Something's better than nothing after all. Just go out and you can observe multiple such events within a day, just find some challenges to watch out for. Where there are challenges, there are people settling.

The reason? I can think of two. One is about what it takes and the other is how does it feel. The feel is good, definitely. I have had that feel quite a few times myself. What do I have to do? I just have to show that I am trying. And there will be people around ready with their "it's okay"s. The "it's okay" feels good, especially if it comes from several people.
The summary, I tried, I failed, people appreciated me.

And I guess that's what we are thriving for. For appreciation and love from people. Sympathy gets confused with love. I start believing that these people like me. Actually they do not, at least not for this stint of mine.

The other reason. I think that's the bigger reason. Because it takes a lot. Among the two components of efforts: On and off the field. On-field efforts bring glory, off-field efforts bring agony. On-field efforts win us appreciation, off-field efforts have big opportunity costs attached to them.
So, we got 2 deals in front of us…and for now, we take out the risk, just to keep the equation simple.
Deal 1: Go all in. Work hard, on the field, and especially, especially off the field. Do 100% of the work, and get 100% rewards.

Deal 2: Work partially. Make on field efforts, which is something like just 5% of the total, and get rewards aka sympathy, which feels like at least 20% of the rewards, at least in the moment, and well, we are short sighted beings, so we are okay with our moment.
Expected values ?
Does it make sense now? I guess it does.

So, why not just make the on field efforts, which is just 5% of the total time, and settle for sympathy, which creates an illusion of partial success. Hard truth, it is not. People appreciate failures. I do it personally. Failures teach you a lot, and more importantly, it takes courage to attempt and fail.

It might sound like I am criticizing both the faces of the coin. But if you think about it, I am criticizing the "willingness to settle". Settling actually means, you didn't have the courage, you didn't attempt, and you did not fail. Embrace failures, for sure do. But do not call settling as failing. Failing is having the courage to try, try, keep trying. You do not accept failure until you fail.                   …. To be continued
Thank you for reading.

emotions.title: Some emotions I don't understand - Ujjwal Mathur
emotions.heading: There are some emotions I don't understand
content: There are a lot of things I don't understand. There are several emotions that I don't understand. There are some scenarios that I don't understand.
I am feeling one of those right now.

I am watching the post-match presentation of the T20 World Cup Final, 2024. India vs South Africa. Close to a billion, literally a billion, people wanted one common thing. I see Irfan Pathan crying in the studio, yes they are airing it. He is nostalgic about the time he won it for India. He is overwhelmed. The celebrations show Rohit Sharma crying, the fans crying, Rahul Dravid smiling, Jasprit Bumrah smiling. Everyone is experiencing a plethora of emotions, everyone is overwhelmed. Even the people who were watching it on their devices. A lot of people shared smiles, a lot of people drained tears. And why won't they? They, everyone who is a citizen, awaited this moment. They wanted their team to lift the silverware. But the wait sort of became eternal when India lost the One Day World Cup on November 19, 2023. We saw the tears back then, for the first time (actually, in the eyes of a lot of people), probably after 2017. The dusk of the Legends Virat and Rohit triggered those emotions, as this was surely the last World Cup the two played together, having won nothing in their legends era. So much so that the word Depression became famous on social media in India probably because of those events.
So, these emotions have a rich history. But there are some outliers I saw.

Virat is not smiling, at least not a smile I feel to be true. It was a made-up smile when he received the Player Of the Match. An explanation might be the announcement of this being his last T20I game.

He has had an outstanding career. I am not someone to speak about that. He is the one guy I so wanted to win this trophy. A big reason I think is the RCB saga, because he hasn't won any trophy since 2013. Rohit has won 5 since then. So, that's an explanation of Virat being the favorite, supported by me being a Virat fan.

Anyway, as soon as I saw that presentation of Virat while receiving that award, my mind rewind to that interview of Virat Kohli where he addressed why he was laughing when he hit his awaited 71st century after 1019 days. He said he laughed, because he couldn't believe this is what he had been waiting for. This is what he was starving for almost 3 years. Everyone criticised him, to the extent that he should be dropped from the team. Can you believe this, drop Virat Kohli from the Indian Team. Yes, this was a serious dining table debate for a long time. People who have followed Cricket for long were, at some point, part of this debate, and many even supported, and in fact justified, the proposal.

But really, I don't understand this. I followed the One Day World Cup 2023 very closely. I had my semester exams before and after the finals, but you know just how important they are, If you have India playing against Australia in a WC final. In fact, I finished my exam early, to watch as much Cricket as possible that day. Like a lot of cricket fans, I wanted India to win so bad that day. But we lost. And that created a void, not just in me, but inside every cricket lover.

And that void, that wound reappeared today, in the hope that it might get replenished. And the result was expected to do that. But now that we have won the silverware, I am not overwhelmed anymore. I don't understand, I don't feel what I was feeling every moment I thought India was losing, when it was 30 off 30, not when Surya got out. I went on a roller coaster throughout the match, but I don't feel a high now. Virat bhai isn't probably feeling that high. He was laughing out of the situation when he hit that century.

That triggered a question in me. Perhaps, we often don't want the high, we just want the void to fill. We don't feel the high or the plateau. There is no plateau in fact. There is either a void or a no void. That very well resembles the psychological concept of loss aversion. We see and feel a loss much more than a gain or win of equivalent volume.

I have felt this before. You might have too maybe. There might have been a time when you wanted something so hard that you made so much effort to get there, but when you get there, you feel like, now what. I am here, now what.
I don't have an answer or even a side to take on this. This is just a speculation. But I do want answers. I will surely write more on this when I have enough.

I don't want to keep the feeling of having that void away from this. I saw Quinton de Kock not crying in 2015. I saw him crying in 2023. I saw him crying today. I saw Captain Markram. The proteas tasted the fluid filling up the void, only to find it digged even deeper. Reminded me of De Villiers crying in 2015. His void never filled. More thanks to the RCB saga. You don't want to experience that void. Ugh.
PS : I have always been a CSK fan.
Tags - Sports, Emotions, Loss aversion.
Thank you for reading.
If you have a take on this, share it with me. I will post it here named or anonymously.
Write to me @newsforujjwalmathur@gmail.com or on X @ujjwalmathur03

expwithsnakes.title: The experiment with children and snakes in a room - Ujjwal Mathur
expwithsnakes.heading: The experiment with children and snakes in a room
content: BBC ran a popular experiment, introducing some infants with snakes. - Watch here

So, the experiment was conducted in a closed room, where the children could not see their parents/caregivers. The children were playing on the floor, and slowly, some snakes were introduced into the room, the snakes being trained and harmless, of course.

You might have seen a 'sapera' or snake charmer come with a snake to your locality, and some of us might have even touched the snake, and we knew of course that the snakes were harmless, unless we wouldn't allow the man to enter the premises. Well, how do our younger siblings react to them? I don't think they would have a fun interaction if they had to touch the snakes, right?
Guess how the newborns reacted to those snakes, or should I say interacted? Well, yeah. They interacted.

As soon as the snakes came around, even with their forked tongues, the young ones tried to find their caregiver for instructions. Where are they? They couldn't find them, so they had to respond on their own. And well, they did. What was seen next was a lot of touching, and holding, and grabbing, and trying to lift the reptiles. And god, I didn't expect that. In fact, I reacted very strangely.
The experiment along with several others made researchers conclude that we are born with no fears at birth. How do we get them?

Remember when the children tried to spot their parents? Yup, right there. Our caregivers, not only provide us with love, food, clothing, and shelter, but also what turn out to be our reflexes. A child, whenever in an unfamiliar situation, looks towards their parent, waiting for the instruction. And, that's how we learn that we have to fear certain things. We keep up adopting behaviors from around to the point that one day we are fearful of being 5 minutes late to a meeting. By the way, we should be on time, but that's not the point :). That's how we even pick up our reflexes.

Fear is one of many emotions we feel, and one of many we pick up from our parents and people around us. This takes me to how a person's childhood shapes their personality. For a long time, I kept this 'fact' in the basket of 'western sycophants' or 'videshi chonchle'. But now that I realise, I just cannot not think about this whenever I see a low tempered or extremely angry guy (not being gender inclusive intentionally here).
I often think I would want to 'cultivate' the childhood experiences of my future children for this very reason. I will keep exploring.
Thank you for reading.

perfectsociety.title: What Would Happen in a Perfect Society? - Ujjwal Mathur
perfectsociety.heading: What Would Happen in a Perfect Society?
content: A Utopia is a fictional or imaginary community or society that is considered to be near-perfect or have highly desirable qualities.
Would you want to be part of a Utopian world? I guess I would be. Until, I read about this experiment.
Several extremely smart people have imagined a Utopian world, what would it look like, what would be the dynamics of such a place?
The Experiment

Well, Biologist John B. Calhoun was one such gentleman. So curious, that he decided to build one. Just not for us, but for mice. Why mice? Because they share more than 98% of DNA with us. So, pretty close. Let's build for them, and see what would happen if humans lived in one, he might have thought.

So, he built a paradise. A place with plenty of resources, food, water, shelter, regular cleaning, suitable temperature, everything but limited space, just as our Earth is. And he brought 4 couples there, selecting the healthiest mice he could.
The Rise and Fall

The experiment started and the species flourished, they enjoyed and started reproducing. By day 315, the population grew to over 600. Now, the resources were not exactly plentiful, and so the population growth slowed. There were more mice than there were social roles, which broke many of them down, and hindered their ability to form social bonds.

Now, there were two kinds of mice. One, that did not fight amongst themselves, and the other that did. Members of the first kind just ate and slept. While the second one, they fought for roles and reproduction, leading to widespread cannibalism, violence, and asexuality. The mouse society had collapsed.
By day 560, the population peaked at 2200. There were fewer pregnancies and the mice had stopped regenerating. The few left who could, the first group, had lost their social ability to do so.
"On day 920 was the last conception, and the last mouse died on day 1766, 4 years and 10 months after colonization."
Calhoun said the mice had died two deaths. One was that of their spirit and the society, and the other was of their physical body.
The Conclusion
A Utopian world led to overpopulation.
Calhoun concluded that overpopulation leads to violence and hypersexual activities, followed by asexuality, self-destruction, and extinction.
No matter how sophisticated we are, which we are contrary to mice, such a scenario leads to the same results.
Final Thought
I guess a perfect world is not so perfect.
Reminds me of a Japanese phrase from the bestseller Ikigai.
"Wabi-Sabi."

quesreligion.title: Ever Questioned Religion? - Ujjwal Mathur
quesreligion.heading: Ever Questioned Religion?
content: This is a thought that dates long long back. But I only got the idea of writing this while talking about this to my friend, in my college dining hall, today.

Reflecting on the earliest memories from my childhood, I cannot recall a version of myself exhibiting faith. Can you recall from your childhood, what was your stance during events of religious significance?

Well, the earliest memory I have is when I was 11 years old. I remember, I had believed that I was an atheist. Why? Because I did not believe in God? How did I know that? Because I had some questions, and I could not find answers, and the best I tried was my friends, my parents, and grandparents. They couldn't answer my questions, and that was my limit, at least I thought it was. So, I started believing that I was an atheist. Oh, they were very logical questions. So logical, that even today I do not have answers to them. It's just that now I am not dumb enough to call myself atheist because of my lack of knowledge.

The questions were simple, how complex could an 11-year-old have thought. But, they seem like questions even today. Religion, irrespective of whether you believe in the beliefs or not, has a lot of hypotheses, and so the questions are going to be hypothetical as well, so please bear with me, and whichever side you belong to, take these as questions from a dumb guy. But do try to answer, as logically as you can, to yourself.
First, why all this suffering?
We keep hearing all these accidents, massacres, catastrophes, crimes and everything. But think of it, if there is someone infinitely powerful, watching all this, why don't they interfere?

"Satyug is the first of the four yugas, or ages, in the Hindu Yuga Cycle. It is considered the most virtuous age, marked by high standards of morality, righteousness, and spirituality. The name 'Satya' means truth."
Why couldn't Satyug last forever? Mythology says that we humans did all bad to us, and came all the way towards this sadist world. But why not take the ability of doing this away from us?
I understand the dumbness of this question. It's just never ever I found an answer that rejected this question with logic. I am waiting to be rejected, just give a fair enough reason.
Draupadi in Mahabharat

I always questioned why didn't Shri Krishna save Draupadi and Pandavas. I know, I know, he saved her from during the Cheer Haran. What happened next? They went into exile for 15 years. And yes, in the end, good won over evil. But what did they do to deserve all those sufferings?
"According to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), 10% of the world's population, or 828 million people, go to bed hungry each night."
"Over 370 million girls and women globally subjected to rape or sexual assault as children" – UNICEF
Why?
I don't understand. If we are the children of God, then why not help?
Coming to Karma

Okay, coming a bit out of the hypotheses. Let me get Karma. Let me get my punishments for whatever bad I have done. But does that justify rapes? The worst, most haunting experience that a person can go through. How can Karma justify this?
Why not bring some order? Why let the Jeffrey Epstein case happen at all?
Final Thoughts

These are just some thoughts. And I don't straightaway call myself an atheist now. I realised knowledge of religion is the first step towards getting answers, and this is going to be a long journey, and I have started that journey.
By the way, my mom did not expect this change in me, reading about religion and mythology. Let's see what I discover.
We should question things. Many of us do. We should then actually look for answers. Rarely, we do.

perspective.title: Understanding Perspectives - Ujjwal Mathur
perspective.heading: Perspectives
perspective.credits: Credits: Andrew Bustamante, Lex Fridman, Henry Ford
content:
This is something I've come across several times.
Andrew Bustamante elaborated on the Lex Fridman Podcast about Perception vs perspective.
Henry Ford famously said,
If there is any one secret of success, it lies in the ability to get the other person's point of view and see things from that person's angle as well as from your own.

Very general statement, but is it that common in practice?
I used to think, "wow, that's a great line, and I know that, so I guess I am smart". Task Done.
I guess not. Knowing that doesn't suffice the purpose of having that in practice. I observed myself, and figured out that I am far away from actually following the great advice by Ford.
I did an (inaccurate) analysis of my peers' behaviour, and seldom did they show this trait. Only one of my many friends, who is a very humble and empathetic guy, showed it to some extent.

I also want to differentiate this from being empathetic as used in the general sense. Empathy is defined as "the ability to imagine how another person is feeling and so understand his/her mood", and used in the sense of understanding someone when they are experiencing a high of emotions.

However, here I want to focus on understanding a person's perspective in everyday situations—whether it's a salesman selling laptops, a carpenter working, or a housemaid cooking.
These are everyday situations without emotional highs, and that's exactly where Ford's insight becomes crucial.

Trying to mentally step into another person's shoes and see the world through their eyes, is what he meant by understanding their perspective "of everything".

As Bustamante said, Everyone has a perception of the world, their "Image" of the world, and it's unique for everyone. But, there is no advantage in that, we don't have any additional information about anyone, and therefore it doesn't help us in "decoding" people and getting along with them.

However, if we try to understand a person's perspective, their lens of looking at the world, and their reason/justifications of acting the way they do, that gives us extra information. Now that we understand the why of that person's behaviour, we have an edge over others, and the use cases, as Bustamante asserted, are immediate and massive in the long run.

I believe this is extremely powerful and as beautiful in practice as it sounds. I will try to follow this for sure, and consciously keep myself in check.
I, Henry Ford and Andrew Bustamante personally recommend everyone to practice it a lot more.
Thank You for reading.
